In Phys.Rev. Lett. 122, 084501 (2019), Esposito et al.
introduce the notion of a gravitational mass M carried
by sound waves as given by:

transverse T) type of sound wave considered. E is sound
wave energy and ρm the mass density of the wave carrier
medium.
They apply this notion to earthquakes and deduce that
for a Richter scale seism of magnitude R = 9 there is an
induced change δg = 10−4 nm/s2 in gravitational accel-
eration, concluding that presently δg is too small to be
measured. However, they point out that it might be pos-
sible soon to detect these changes since a considerable
progress has been achieved recently with the detection of
gravitational waves with the LIGO experiment [2].
Surprisingly, Esposito et al. have, in fact, hinted at
an acoustic version of Einstein formula E = Mc2

An earthquake releases energies through various chan-
nels such as heat, radiation or frictional weakening and
inelastic deformation processes in rocks leading e.g. to
formation of cracks.
Presently, the characterization of
seisms is based on moment-magnitude scale [3] which is
more accurate than the Richter scale especially in the
case of strong earthquakes.
In the Richter scale, quake energy is obtained from
the Gutenberg-Richter [3] formula E
=
101.5×R+4.8,
while in the moment-magnitude Mw scale, it is given by
E = 101.5×Mw+4.32. This allows us to plot simultane-
ously versus Mw, the gravitational acceleration change
and seism energy as displayed in ﬁg 1.
According to the graph, the strongest quake (Mw=10)
produces δg = 10−3 nm/s2 slightly below the current
sensitivity 10−2 nm/s2 of superconducting gravimeters.
By comparison, the Sumatra-Andaman quake [4] is
one of the strongest ever recorded over the last 65 years.
